104.body: "Swear not at all" is not about bad language. Peterson reads it as a warning against claiming to stand for moral principles you cannot actually carry. Be wary of anyone who swears he acts on the highest principle. A more honest stance is: here is what I am aiming at, I am probably wrong somewhere, point it out. Letting your yes be yes and your no be no is a call to simple speech, offering neither more than you can deliver nor nothing. In an argument, he adds, work out what would actually satisfy you, and ask the other person the same. He ends with a warning about loud claims to speak for the poor: poverty is rarely caused only by a lack of money.

105.body: Do not swear by God that you will do good; who are you to carry that burden? You should distrust someone who swears he acts on the highest principle. Better: 'Here's what I'm aiming at. I'm probably an idiot. Point it out.' In an argument, figure out what would satisfy you, and ask the other person. Simplicity of speech: do not offer more than you can, but not nothing. Poverty is rarely caused by lack of money; a client was fine until his disability check brought predatory friends.

111.body: "An eye for an eye" sounds brutal, but Peterson points out that in its time it was a limit: take no more than was taken. Christ pushes further with turning the other cheek and going the extra mile. He treats the extra mile as a practical rule that keeps working when it is repeated, though not to the point of martyrdom. In business it means delivering faster, better and more reliably than expected, and never annoying your customers. A critic may be a canary in the coal mine, warning you of something real, and an enemy you win over often becomes your best ally. How do you know your enemy is not trying to improve you?

112.body: Proportional retaliation was a real limit on vengefulness. Going the extra mile is an extremely useful iterative ethical principle, though not to the point of martyrdom. In business: deliver faster, at a reasonable price, at higher quality than expected. Rule number one: do not annoy your customers; one annoyed customer can cost a million people's goodwill. A rude video store owner went out of business in three months after Peterson's disagreeable friend called him out. A complaining customer may be a canary in the coal mine; respond and you may convert him. An enemy converted is a better ally; how do you know your enemy is not trying to improve you?

118.body: Peterson starts from a plain wish: it would be better not to have enemies, and wishing them suffering makes nothing better. Loving your enemies means wanting them not to be enemies, of you, of themselves, or of life, and trying to bring them into the fold. That is not naive. Between naive trust, which gets burned, and cynicism, which makes cooperation impossible, he describes courageous trust: extending goodwill while knowing people can be dangerous. Peacemaking takes fine judgment, as anyone who sets limits for a three-year-old knows. "Be ye perfect" he reads as "aim right": you may miss, but you can aim at the highest target, and it is facing the worst that calls out the best in you.

119.body: Wishing enemies hotter in hell does not make anything better. Love enemies by wanting them not to be enemies, of you, of themselves, or of being. Peacemaking means making very fine discriminations, as with a three-year-old's boundaries. Naive trust gets burned, cynicism makes trade impossible; courageous trust extends goodwill knowing everyone is full of snakes. With a paranoid client with four restraining orders, nothing beat honesty; you cannot fool a career psychopath. Be perfect: maybe you cannot hit the target, but you can aim right. The shaman confers with ancestors; rescue your dead father from the belly of the beast. It's only the worst that calls for the best.

125.body: Matthew 6 opens with a warning against doing good to be seen, which Peterson calls an injunction against virtue signalling. Be at least a little sceptical of your own motives. Young people feel a real urge to save the world, he says, but they are often told to do it by protesting before they have disciplined themselves. His favourite definition of Christian charity is productivity plus generosity. Not letting your left hand know what your right hand is doing means keeping good deeds secret even from yourself, so you do not puff yourself up or let your status rise beyond your competence. He spends time on how narcissists and psychopaths fake goodness to win reputation, and warns that naivety dressed up as virtue is an invitation to exploitation.

126.body: From lecture section 24: Do Not Your Alms Before Men: Virtue Signaling (Matthew 6:1) The 'do not pray in public' injunction is an injunction against virtue signaling. Be skeptical of your own motives; do good in secret to avoid moral hazard. Piaget: morality emerges from repeated games, and late adolescence brings a messianic urge to find your place. Peer groups are a bridge from parents to autonomy; a star who is not a team player is a skilled narcissist. Students waste a median of 8 hours a day, roughly $150,000 a year at $50 an hour, yet are told to be moral avatars. The best definition of Christian charity: productivity and generosity. From lecture section 25: Let Not Thy Left Hand Know: Narcissism, Psychopathy and Naivety (Matthew 6:2-5) Do not let your status rise beyond your competence. Keep good deeds secret even from yourself, because you will aggrandize yourself. Psychopathy is not a path to success: failure to learn from experience, short-term hedonic priority. Psychopaths betray themselves as much as others and become drifters because people warn each other. At protests, a few men are there to exploit the young women: serious predators. About 1 percent of criminals commit about 70 percent of crimes.

132.body: Church, Peterson says, is for penitents, not for status. The private prayer he recommends is a question: what am I doing that is stupid and wrong, that I could change, and that I would change? Ask it honestly and the answer comes. Start small: a client who could not face cleaning his room began with a quarter of one sock drawer, and progress then grew quickly. On vain repetitions, he says God is not impressed by volume. Real prayer is close to real thinking: you ask a genuine question and an answer appears that you did not have before. The more genuine the question, the better the answer. But answers must be tested, so bring in people who disagree and let them hammer on your idea.

133.body: From lecture section 26: Enter Into Thy Closet: Private Prayer and Small Steps (Matthew 6:5-6) The Jesus prayer reminds you that you are a sinner, not a moral paragon; church is a penitentiary. Going to church despite doctrinal doubts signals willingness to subordinate yourself to a shared enterprise. The simple prayer: what am I doing that is stupid and wrong, that I could change, that I would change. In an argument, ask what you did to make it likely, even if the other person is 95 percent wrong. The client left the vacuum diagonally across the threshold for a week; the hero first meeting the giant often runs. Start with something humble enough: one quarter of one sock drawer; progress then becomes exponential. From lecture section 27: Use Not Vain Repetitions: Thinking as Prayer (Matthew 6:7-8) God is not impressed by sheer volume of communication. Your Father knows what you need; the task is to open yourself to revelation. If you think, you pray: you ask a question and get an answer you did not have. Jung: thoughts appear in the theater of imagination like a table when you walk into a room. Do not write an essay about something you do not care about; it is a lie from the beginning. Paranoid people are deluded by the force of their own thoughts; revelation must be tested.

138.title: The verses

139.body: Peterson walks through the prayer line by line. Heaven may be the place you are in when you are doing the right thing at the right time. To hallow something is to put it in the highest place, and if nothing is sacred you have no priorities, which feels like anxiety. "Thy kingdom come" is the moment when time disappears because you are fully absorbed; the task is to spend more of your life there. "Thy will be done" means letting the highest value run all the way down, from God to community to family to you. What you most need is often found where you least want to look, and challenges you choose feel completely different from ones forced on you. "Forgive us our debts as we forgive our debtors" is reciprocity, not blanket absolution. "Lead us not into temptation" is humility about your limits: if you are quitting drinking, skip the party. The closing verses on forgiveness tie your inner judge, your conscience, to how you treat others.

14.body: Speaker: Jordan B. Peterson, lecture series on the Sermon on the Mount, delivered over four days (Day 1: Matthew 5:1–16; Day 2: 5:17–48; Day 3: Matthew 6; Day 4: Matthew 7). Peterson reads from the King James Version. Transcript: a private transcript of about 80,845 words, kept in a local study wiki (~/wikis/sermon-on-the-mount/, file source/sermon_full.txt). That wiki splits the transcript into 50 contiguous sections in lecture order, each with a summary, key ideas, exact quotes with word positions, and questions. Its coverage audit confirms the 50 sections cover every word with no gaps or overlaps. How this wiki was made from it: the 50 sections were merged into 27 passage pages that follow the sermon's verse order. Four sections (19, 20, 31, 34) cross a passage boundary and are split between two pages. The "Peterson's reading" text on each page is a new plain-language summary; key ideas and questions come from the section notes; quotes are copied exactly from the transcript and limited to short excerpts. Word positions ("about word N") count words from the start of the transcript and are approximate. Gaps: five verses are never read aloud or discussed on their own: 5:9, 5:12, 5:45, 7:8 and 7:18. See the verse map .

140.body: From lecture section 28: Our Father, Hallowed Be Thy Name, Thy Kingdom Come (Matthew 6:9-10) Heaven may be the spirit that shines through every level of a properly ordered hierarchy. Even severe depression varies; find when you are less miserable and practice being there. There is nothing worse than traveling efficiently down the wrong road. If everything is equally important, everything is equally meaningless and you are anxious. From lecture section 29: Thy Will Be Done, Daily Bread, Forgive Us Our Debts (Matthew 6:10-12) Thy will be done means propagating the highest value down from God to state, city, community, family and individual. If your life is trivial and you are bored, you are not doing anything meaningful. Your salvation may be found in your problems: what you most need is where you least want to look. Horrible things find you wherever you hide, and we are an unbroken chain of creatures who managed the worst. From lecture section 30: Lead Us Not Into Temptation: The Desert and the Zone (Matthew 6:13) Pray not to face temptations beyond your ability to control; know where not to go. Abandoning your tyrannical presuppositions takes you into the desert, not straight to the promised land. Up the mountain, down into the valley, up a higher mountain: no mountain to mountain without chaos. If you stay open to incremental improvement, revelations become small, interesting revolutions. From lecture section 31: If You Forgive Men Their Trespasses, and Fasting (Matthew 6:14-18) Your conscience calls you out and you cannot simply tell it what to do. The Holy Spirit may manifest as conscience, the judge within. If you are harshly judgmental to raise your own moral status, your conscience will torture you in precise proportion. You can get to love of yourself through love of others, for example by treating yourself well for your kids' sake. Forgiveness is not the absence of judgment; walk the child through what was right and what to improve. Letting kids rule at three is demoralizing; show them adulthood is better. Peter Pan keeps his magic but never gets Wendy.

146.body: Peterson reads the fasting verses as a warning against false martyrdom: "look how much I am suffering for you." That kind of display blames others for your sacrifices and then uses them as proof of moral superiority. The hypocrites "have their reward", and he notes the line is a joke: the reward is only the attention. The alternative is to wash your face and look put-together when you are giving something up. Like giving and prayer, fasting is turned inward, done for the Father who sees in secret rather than for an audience.

King James Version (1769) World English Bible 19 Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt, and where thieves break through and steal: “Don’t lay up treasures for yourselves on the earth, where moth and rust consume, and where thieves break through and steal; 20 But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt, and where thieves do not break through nor steal: but lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust consume, and where thieves don’t break through and steal; 21 For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also. for where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.
152.title: The verses

153.body: This is not a condemnation of wealth, Peterson insists. Despising abundance is foolish when much of the world still lacks it. But money does not solve the deep problems of life: your marriage, your parents' decline, your own death. The treasure moth and rust cannot touch is character, which protects you better than wealth and also generates it. Hunter-gatherers stored future food in their reputations by sharing their kills and playing down their luck, and that kind of treasure does not rot or get stolen. You will often face a choice between character and wealth, and where your treasure is shows in which one you pick.

154.body: Being rich does not fix your marriage, death, or your parents' decline. You are a fool if you despise abundance; a billion people still burn dung. Character is a better protection against catastrophe than wealth, and conscientiousness predicts success. Sacrificing character for wealth is a bad trade, because you want wealth to get what only character delivers. Surrounded by people who love you, you ride out political and social chaos best. Good hunters downplay their luck and give away the best cuts, storing future food in reputation. Reputation does not rot and is not stolen. Where your treasure is: you will choose between character and wealth often, maybe daily.

160.body: Peterson treats vision and attention as primary. What you aim at decides what you see: name your aim and the world lays itself out as paths that help you and obstacles that get in the way, with feelings to match. Positive emotion says "path open"; negative emotion says "stop" or "danger". Sin, in the Greek, is an archery word meaning to miss the target, or to have no target at all. If the eye is single, aimed at the good, the whole body is full of light. If the eye is evil, the darkness has no bottom: Hitler, he says, ended up exactly where he was aiming.

161.body: Primates with the best vision live among the most poisonous snakes; we see color to find ripe fruit. Thought follows attention; attention is primary and reveals your hierarchy of values. Specify your aim and the world reveals affordances and obstacles; objects are what object. Positive emotion means pathway open; negative emotion means stop or danger. Sin, hamartia, is an archery term: to miss the target, or to have none. The eye on the pyramid is not part of the pyramid; what is at the top is above the hierarchy. Human eye whites signal attention; a shared vision aligns people so they can compete without conflict. Hitler ended exactly where he aimed; however miserable you are, there is a stupid thing that can make it worse.

167.body: No one can serve two masters. Peterson reads this as a call to one integrated aim at the top of your values, rather than several that pull against each other. Mammon means wealth and the desire for security, but he stresses that this is not an anti-capitalist teaching, and not a call to misery either: Christ turns water into wine at a wedding, and paradise may be a feast. Constraints you choose are there to make you disciplined, productive and generous, and real mastery shows itself in being able to handle even grim things with humour.

175.body: "Consider the lilies" can sound like a drop-out ethic: stop working and drift. Peterson says the passage turns on faith instead. Obsessive worry about security, and even an obsessive sense of duty, can reflect a lack of faith. The answer is in "seek ye first the kingdom": aim at the highest possible good in every way, and the rest is added. Your real interest stretches across time and includes other people. If your aim is right and your words are true, you can stop worrying and give full attention to the present, trusting that the larger picture is in order.

182.body: Matthew 7 opens with "Judge not, that ye be not judged." Peterson notes that it does not exactly say "do not judge"; it says the measure you use will be used on you. Criticism in its real sense means separating the wheat from the chaff, not tearing things down. Any ideal judges you, and you can close the gap either by moving toward the good or by trying to destroy it, as Cain did with Abel. The mote and the beam: students who dismiss great thinkers over one flaw are ignoring the beam in their own eye. Even a harsh critic can hand you the useful five percent if you listen. Few people, he quotes Carl Rogers, have the moral courage to listen. Clear your own vision first; only then can you help someone else see.

183.body: From lecture section 36: Judge Not, That Ye Be Not Judged (Matthew 7:1-2) It does not exactly say do not judge; Revelation's Christ judges most harshly those who play both ends against the middle. Read to learn: criticism means separating the wheat from the chaff, not denigration; read Freud despite Victorian assumptions. Noah was 'a wise man in his generations': as good as a person could be for his time. Jung: dreams compensate for gaps in conscious understanding; categories loosen in dreams. Any ideal is a judge; you close the gap by moving toward the good or by destroying the good, as Cain did. Without an ideal there is only anxiety and no joy; humility in faith mediates between you and the ideal. From lecture section 37: The Mote and the Beam (Matthew 7:3-5) Feeling morally superior to Nietzsche is a convenient accomplishment for a 19-year-old. Even if criticism is 95 percent vitriol, the 5 percent may fix something you would not otherwise fix. Your most vicious enemy can be your best friend because they go after subtle things. Talk to people who think differently and ask how they came to their view. Rogers: people generally don't have the moral courage to listen. You cannot act as a moral social agent until you clear your own vision.

189.body: "Do not give what is holy to dogs" means do not waste what is precious on someone not ready for it. Peterson reads it as a lesson in listening. If someone is not taking in what you say, you are probably pitching it at the wrong level, or you are not talking to who you think you are: perhaps to a frightened ten-year-old part of them, or to your own projection. So stop talking. In therapy he lets people speak until they are ready to listen, and uses Rogers' method: summarise what they said until they agree you have it right. Tension drains away and the useless parts fall off. Healing, he says, is not just letting feelings out; it is updating your map of the world so the past does not repeat.

190.body: 'Do not cast pearls before swine' means do not waste what is holy on what is unfit for it. When troubled people do not take advice, you are pitching above their position. If someone is not listening, you are not where you think you are and not talking to who you think. Partial subpersonalities: sometimes you are talking to a part of someone that is ten years old. A client needed to talk 45 minutes per session; over ten years that dropped to 15 and she was doing stand-up comedy. If someone is not listening, shut up; doubling down never works clinically. Rogers: listen, then summarize to their satisfaction; tension drains and chaff falls away. Healing is not catharsis; it is updating the map so you are prepared and the past does not repeat.

197.body: Ask and it shall be given: the chance of getting what you want without asking is close to zero. Peterson says many people hide what they want in a fog so they never have to risk asking, and then blame others for missing a target they never named. Seeking means watching yourself honestly, noticing when you are less miserable and doing more of that, and following what beckons. "If his son ask bread, will he give him a stone?" leads him to biology. You are adapted to the world well enough to be alive, so opening yourself to learning should work, but you will not find out unless you go all in; faith has to come before the evidence. A small request, like asking a new neighbour a favour, opens relationships. "If ye then, being evil, know how to give good gifts" becomes the idea that each person is a small model of the cosmos, and that a sincere question tends to receive an answer.

198.body: From lecture section 39: Ask, Seek, Knock (Matthew 7:7-8) A halo is a sun or moon behind the figure of value; the crown of thorns may be a solar image. Being vague about wants lets you punish your partner for missing a target they never saw. From lecture section 40: If His Son Asks Bread, Will He Give Him a Stone? Adaptation and Faith (Matthew 7:9-10) The question is whether you can trust the fundamental substructure of reality. Biologically, you are adapted at least enough to live and reproduce, so learning and transformation should work. You are a repertoire of biologically instantiated possibility; the gym shows capacity drawn out in proportion to effort. The upper limit is unknown; people who seem to do six impossible things maximize their potential. From lecture section 41: Good Gifts, the Microcosm, and the Yoga Client (Matthew 7:11) Dawkins sent Peterson a paper saying an organism must be a microcosm of its environment. From a bird you could infer air, gravity and temperature on Earth. If you were not a microcosm of the cosmos you could not live in it; that is both a biological and a religious answer. Kenosis means emptying: Christ as a thumbnail of God, bounded in time and place as a carpenter.

203.body: v. King James Version (1769) World English Bible 12 Therefore all things whatsoever ye would that men should do to you, do ye even so to them: for this is the law and the prophets. Therefore, whatever you desire for men to do to you, you shall also do to them; for this is the law and the prophets.
203.title: The verses

204.body: "Whatsoever ye would that men should do to you, do ye even so to them: for this is the law and the prophets." Peterson calls it a direct instruction: work out exactly how you would like to be treated, then do that to others first. That is the price. If you treat others in the best possible way, you are already doing the best thing, so in a sense you win the game. He then widens it. Life will bring suffering, so the better stance is not grudging acceptance but "celebratory acceptance: bring it on." Joy and suffering may be tied together, and a great adventure may be better than mere happiness. A garden with a snake may even be a better garden, because you learn how to handle snakes. The golden rule turns tradition into a living principle of careful, judicious reciprocity.

205.body: From lecture section 42: Do Unto Others: The Law and the Prophets, Ultimate Sacrifice (Matthew 7:12) 'How good could things get if you put yourself together?' The law is custom and tradition, Osiris, necessary, wise and dead; it must ally with the prophetic voice. Multiple characterizations of the divine imply a central essence; Christ names it as the golden rule. Figure out how you would like to be treated, then do it to others first; it is a direct instruction. If you treat others in the best possible manner you are already doing the best thing: you win the game. Most parents would die for their children; that is the fundamental relationship. From lecture section 43: Bring It On: Joy and Suffering, Adventure, the Serpent and the Tyrant (Matthew 7:12 (continued)) You are going to face all of it, so accept it: 'celebratory acceptance. Bring it on.' Nietzsche: imagine joy and suffering are proportionate and tied together. Profound music like Beethoven's Ninth goes from the tragic depths to the pinnacle; mere happiness is insipid elevator music. God calls Abraham to war, famine and tyranny, yet it is a great adventure, maybe better than happy. The pirate friend, a lone round-the-world sailor, is hired to fire narcissists in corrupt corporations and enjoys it; better than a nice guy. Do you want to be harmless or something to contend with? You do not get that without accepting the whole catastrophe.

219.body: Wolves in sheep's clothing: Peterson says the most effective disguise of a predator is compassion. Narcissists and psychopaths use your compassion against you by claiming a moral virtue they have not earned. "Ye shall know them by their fruits" he links to a rule from psychoanalysis: if you cannot understand someone's motive, look at the result and infer the aim. Once is an accident, twice a bad day, three times a pattern. Every good tree brings forth good fruit, so the whole tree has to be healthy. He describes a medieval painting in which Eve hands out apples of death beside a skull while Mary hands out the bread of life beside the cross, and draws the lesson that accepting death is the cure for death. Verse 18, "A good tree cannot bring forth evil fruit", is not read aloud; its point is folded into his reading of verses 17 and 19-20.

226.body: Saying "Lord, Lord" is not enough. Peterson says faith is not mainly a statement about what you believe; it is in the doing, acted out in the world. That is why Christianity stresses incarnation, the word taking on flesh, and why Christ is a carpenter, as hands-on as it gets. Pointing to your prophesying and good works is not enough either, especially if those works are really for your own glory. The kingdom, he says, is a real psychological and social state you can live in, and the sermon is a practical guide to getting there.

227.body: Modern rationalists think you just have to say that you believe. Saying it doesn't doom you, but it is no certain indication of salvation. The fundamental essence is 'but he that doeth': an existential emphasis, the imitation of Christ. The word takes on determinate form: incarnation; Christ is a carpenter, as hands-on as it gets. Pointing to your achievements as evidence of ethical wondrousness is the temptation of the aristocracy. The kingdom of God is a psychological and social state you can actually inhabit; this is a practical guide. Mere propositional faith fails, and so does piling up good works for your own benefit.

234.body: What is the rock? Peterson answers: the crucifixion, the full acceptance of tragedy and malice, and building a character strong enough to withstand it. It works like exposure therapy. Walk through the worst before it happens and you are ready when it comes, and perhaps it then does not happen at all. He has seen people face the death of someone they love bravely: they still suffer the loss, but it is not hell. Sorting things out with your parents before their last years, for example, lets you care for them without bitterness. Sand is scattered multiplicity, not unity. When the house falls, the question is whether the storm did it, or whether you were not ready. How prepared can you get?

People who confront death bravely still suffer the loss, but it isn't hell; they transmute it. Sort things out with your parents before their final stages and you can shepherd them without bitterness. Sand is multiplicity, not unity. 241.body: The people were astonished at both what was said and how it was said. Peterson describes astonishment as being overwhelmed by the intensity of the light. Christ taught "as one having authority, and not as the scribes": the authority of someone who lives what he says, set against mere rule-keeping. With this the series ends.

277.body: Peterson reads the sermon almost verse by verse. Checking each KJV verse against the transcript, these five are never read out or discussed on their own: Matthew 5:9 , "Blessed are the peacemakers." The reading jumps from 5:8 to 5:10. Peacemaking comes up later, under Love Your Enemies . Matthew 5:12 , "Rejoice, and be exceeding glad... for so persecuted they the prophets." The idea is covered in the discussion of 5:10–11. Matthew 5:45 , "He maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good." Peterson reads 5:44 and 5:46–48 around it. Matthew 7:8 , "For every one that asketh receiveth." Covered by the discussion of 7:7. Matthew 7:18 , "A good tree cannot bring forth evil fruit." Covered by the discussion of 7:17 and 7:19–20. Smaller skips: 5:1–2 is treated as the setting, and the first half of 6:32 ("for after all these things do the Gentiles seek") is passed over. Every other verse is read aloud and commented on.

3.body: Peterson reads the sermon line by line as practical psychology, not as a list of doctrines. It begins on a mountain because the first rule is to aim up, at the highest good you can conceive. From there: admit what you do not know, tell the truth, and take on burdens voluntarily, because that is what builds you. Judgment moves from outcome to intent, so anger and lust count, and reconciliation comes before worship. Do good, pray and fast in secret rather than for status. Put one aim at the top and stop worrying. Clear your own eye before judging anyone else, ask for what you want, and treat others as you want to be treated, going first. Faith is shown in what you do, not what you say, and the house built on rock is the character that has already faced catastrophe before it arrives.

55.body: Before he reads a single blessing, Peterson asks why the sermon is given on a mountain. His answer is that height is the oldest symbol of seeing far and aiming high. From the top you can see where you are going, so the first rule is simple: aim up. He argues that most good feeling in life comes from seeing yourself make progress toward a worthwhile goal, not from reaching it. Without an aim, and an ethical one, you cannot feel much that is positive at all. Since you are betting your life on what you do anyway, you might as well bet it on the highest good you can imagine. He links this to taking on heavy responsibility on purpose, which he says is the real source of self-respect, and to taking on challenges voluntarily, which builds you up rather than turning you into something that hides.

56.body: Enlightenment happens on a mountain, not in a valley, because from above you can see; the eye of Horus, the falcon and Zazu in The Lion King carry the same symbol. The word that is true and oriented by love brings habitable order out of chaos, and people participate in that with their own speech. Most positive emotion comes from seeing progress toward a goal, not from attaining it; without an ethical aim you cannot experience positive emotion. God classically defined as the summum bonum, the sum of all good things, is a definition, not a statement of belief. You are betting your life on your actions anyway, so why bet it on anything less than the highest good. Bearing a heavy responsibility is the only real answer to the burden of your own flaws, and service to others is one of the deepest pleasures of life. Voluntary challenge turns on new genes and builds new parts of you; fleeing a challenge turns you into a prey animal. Betrayal, death and old age are coming, so you had better be set up for the challenge.

62.body: Peterson takes the blessings one at a time and reads each as a description of a person who is set up to grow. Poor in spirit and meek both mean the opposite of narcissistic: humble enough to admit what you do not know. Security built on walls fails, he says, because the serpent always gets into the garden, so your stability has to rest on competence, and competence starts with making friends with the unknown. Pride of intellect, Milton's Lucifer, is the warning case. Those that mourn are people who let grief in fully; he tells how his father-in-law was transformed by years of caring for his dying wife, and says mourning is proportionate to love. Hunger and thirst after righteousness means wanting the right path enough to pay for it with work and truthful speech; what redeems a life is not happiness but its adventure. The merciful is a reciprocity idea: give a little more than is expected, be the 55-45 player, and doors open that you did not know existed. The pure in heart are free of contempt, including contempt for themselves, and admitting your faults is what brings relief. The persecuted are sharpened by opposition; ideas worth living by should be tested in battle. Verse 9, "Blessed are the peacemakers", is not read aloud in the lecture; Peterson touches on peacemaking later, under loving your enemies.

63.body: From lecture section 2: Blessed Are the Poor in Spirit (Matthew 5:1-3) Poor in spirit does not mean lacking energy; it means blessed are those who are the antithesis of narcissistic. You know a place when what you do there works; the unknown is where your actions no longer match the situation. The serpent always gets into the walled garden, so stability has to depend on competence, not security. From lecture section 3: Blessed Are They That Mourn (Matthew 5:4) Dell Roberts, an extroverted 'Dean Martin' type, unexpectedly became a devoted caregiver over 15 years of his wife's Alzheimer's-type illness. Because he did not shield himself from grief, it transformed him and widened his character. His wife suffered less; it was still hell, but not the lowest depths. From lecture section 4: Blessed Are the Meek (Matthew 5:5) Meek is a restatement of poor in spirit: not arrogant and narcissistic. Milton portrays Lucifer, the light-bringer, as the highest angel gone wrong: rationality that elevates its own pretensions to the status of God. The Tower of Babel is a structure built to replace God, and the result is that no one can communicate. From lecture section 5: Hunger and Thirst After Righteousness (Matthew 5:6) The impediments: you are bitter and resentful, you would rather aim down, and you want the benefits of being good without the work. Pay attention to what you say and you can feel whether each word makes you weaker or stronger. Work is sacrifice: it gives up the present for the future; not sacrificing still means sacrificing the future to the present. From lecture section 6: Blessed Are the Merciful: Reciprocity (Matthew 5:7) Dell's care for his wife led him to a new partner and to children who came to admire him. Caring for the old is reciprocity with your future self: that's you, man. If you deliver more than people expect, you get back more than you expect; work 10 percent longer and earn 40 percent more. From lecture section 7: Blessed Are the Pure in Heart (Matthew 5:8) Pure means not contaminated, not disgusting; it does not mean safe. Eye-rolling contempt is the best predictor of divorce within a year. Self-disgust tells you that you are doing something shameful; Peterson stopped drinking because he drank to misbehave with a good conscience. From lecture section 8: Blessed Are the Persecuted (Matthew 5:10-12) When you improve, people around you (a pathological family, drinking friends) push back. A doubt only stops you if it echoes a doubt you already have; overcoming it strengthens commitment. You do not want your six-year-old playing three-year-olds; opposition sharpens.

69.body: Salt preserves food, but above all it adds flavour: it turns something good into something delightful. Peterson says the same savour shows in Christ's quick, truthful answers to trick questions, in comedians who have to tell the truth to be funny, and in the court fool, the one person free to say what is so. Anyone who is an enemy of the fool is a tyrant. The city on a hill joins the mountain image to community: you climb so you can join others who have climbed. Treating your future self well and treating other people well turn out to be the same skill. A candle on a candlestick means being good in a way that makes others want to copy you. Light draws attention and attention leads to imitation, so do good in the open when people need the example, not to show off. The proper jihad is a competition between invitations, not conversion by the sword. If what you are doing is good, do it in public because people need the example, not to brag. From lecture section 12: The Candle Between Two People, Imitation and Awe (Matthew 5:14-16 (continued)) The light between the spouses, the truth from honest dialogue, is what is superordinate in a marriage. Eve means 'beneficial adversary'; opponent processing gives precision, like two muscles moving a hand smoothly. Treat your partner as you; you are stuck with each other. 76.body: Christ says he has come to fulfil the law, not destroy it. Peterson reads this as the partnership between two forces every person and society needs: the law (habit, tradition, what already works) and the prophet (the voice that updates it when the world changes). Neither is enough alone. Discipline is not the enemy of creativity; like a concert pianist, you go through discipline to reach freedom. "One jot or one tittle" leads him to unfulfilled potential. What you fail to bring out of yourself becomes a source of guilt, and what bothers you most may be your calling. "Whosoever shall do and teach" puts doing first: belief shows in action, not in statements. Exceeding the scribes and Pharisees means being better than a clever lawyer or a showy priest, keeping the spirit of the law and not only its letter.

77.body: From lecture section 13: Think Not That I Am Come to Destroy the Law (Matthew 5:17) Pageau: Barabbas was also called Jesus in one tradition, so the crowd chooses Jesus the revolutionary over Jesus the prophet. From lecture section 14: One Jot or One Tittle: Potential and Responsibility (Matthew 5:18) Gospel of Thomas: you will be destroyed by what you do not reveal within yourself. Parents hate to see children betray who they could be, and discipline should stop it. Potential is not actual, yet failing it produces real guilt and shame. Alternative to Cain's complaint: the cosmos is flawed in proportion to your unwillingness to bring forth what is within you. From lecture section 15: Whosoever Shall Do and Teach Them (Matthew 5:19) 'Do and then teach': faith is not propositional assent; deciding to walk up the hill despite the evidence is the statement of faith. Rogers (a missionary who lost his faith) taught congruence: what you do, feel, aim at and say all line up. People worth listening to are the same in private and in public; there is no show. If your attention wanders with someone, listen harder; that calls out the interesting. From lecture section 16: Exceed the Righteousness of the Scribes and Pharisees (Matthew 5:20) You must be more moral than a priest and more moral than a lawyer. Corrupt lawyers subvert justice by using the law, justified with Luciferian rationalism. 'Point to what I did wrong' can hide an unclean spirit. 83.body: "Thou shalt not kill" becomes "do not even be angry with your brother without cause." Peterson calls this one of the great turns in Western law: judgment moves from outcome to intent. Intent-based justice is harsher in one way, but it also makes mercy possible, because an accident is not a crime. He warns that accusations come back on the accuser, and that judging by impact alone wipes out the very idea of a defence. Leaving your gift at the altar to reconcile with your brother is, he says, the root of his "clean your room" advice: fix what is close to home before you try to save the world. Agreeing with your adversary quickly means taking correction while you are still on the road together, because conflict put off is conflict multiplied. "Till thou hast paid the uttermost farthing" means you get away with nothing; reality is what you cannot distort.

Solve your own moral problems first and you become able to solve family and social ones. From lecture section 19: Agree With Thine Adversary Quickly and the Uttermost Farthing (Matthew 5:25-28) Peterson admits he does not fully understand the verse and reasons it out: the adversary is testing you. He would rather be corrected than right. A messy house is littered with arguments that never happened; divorce drags 30,000 unsolved problems to the next partner. There is a small proportion of truly exploitative people; most partners are no worse than you. Marriage is Jung's alchemical container: because no one can run away, you can reveal yourself and not be alone in hell. Reality is what you cannot distort; payment deferred is payment multiplied. 9.body: The sermon starts on a mountain because you should aim up. Aim at the highest good and that aim fills you with something like enthusiasm, which in Greek means being filled with God. Admit what you do not know, speak the truth, and pick up your burdens on purpose. Judge your own intent, not just your outcomes, and make peace with your brother before anything else. Do good in secret, put one aim at the top, and stop worrying. Look at your own faults before other people's, ask for what you want, and treat others how you want to be treated, starting first. Act out what you believe rather than just saying it. Face catastrophe before it comes and you are the house on the rock: the storm still comes, but you do not fall.
9.title: One-minute version

90.body: Peterson reads the adultery verses as a second, harsher example of the shift from outcome to intent. If you would sleep around but cannot because no one wants you, the absence of the act is no proof of virtue. He leaves it to the listener to decide whether that standard is right, but he is clear that this is what the line means. "If thy right eye offend thee, pluck it out" he reads as sacrificing a part to save the whole. Everyone runs a model of the world, and learning means letting part of that model die. Often the thing you value most is the biggest obstacle to moving forward, which is why the example is the right eye and the right hand. His summary: die a little all the time, so you do not have to die a lot, or completely.

91.body: From lecture section 20: If Thy Right Eye Offend Thee, and Divorce (Matthew 5:29-32) You always run a model of the world; learning means retooling it, so no progress without death and repentance. Often what you value most is the biggest impediment; that is why the example is the right eye and right hand. Die a little all the time so you do not die a lot or completely. Thought is a sacrificial process: create avatars of yourself and let them die instead of you. Out of the tyranny you go into the desert, which is not obviously better. Also in this passage Looking with lust is judged like the act itself: the same move from outcome to intent as the verses on anger. Not sleeping around because no one is interested is not virtue if the desire is still there.

97.body: Peterson calls this "a rough one for modern people" and says plainly that he is not the authority to rule on whether divorce is allowed. What he offers is Jung's view that marriage only works as a real vow: if there is an escape route, you will take it at exactly the moment you should be changing instead. He balances this with a case from his practice, a client married to someone willing to burn everything down, whom he spent years helping. His conclusion is not a rule about divorce but a description of commitment: if you are not all in, you are not married.
